subtopic: TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we were deeply grieved to learn of the death of Mr. Georges Pompidou, President of the French Republic.
The range of his talents, the variety of his careers had made him known to Canadians much before his accession to the presidency of the Republic. A man of letters, high official, financier and politician, success had become rightly familiar to him. President of the Republic since 1969, he had won renown for his particularly intense activities in the field of international relations as well as on the national scene. Thus the influence of his action expanded beyond the French borders.
Tried by illness, he recently gave to all of us the example of a sense of duty which brought out the stamp of his character.

President Pompidou's death will be regretted by Canadians. His moderation and realism, qualities which he owes as much to his origins as to his wide and worldly experience, have been reflected in relations between France and Canada. Under President Pompidou our relations have developed within a framework of concrete co-operation. I am sure that this House and the Canadian people join me in offering our deepest sympathy to the family of President Pompidou, to the government of France and to the French people-a people to whom we are closely linked by language, by culture and, above all, by friendship.
I should like to add, Mr. Speaker, that on behalf of the government and the people of Canada I shall be attending the funeral ceremonies in Paris. At this time I should also like to apologize to those Canadians in Saskatchewan and in Ottawa who will be forced to see me postpone events in which I was to partake with them.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, France is mourning today the loss of its president. Mr. Georges Pompidou was a great statesman. He devoted most of his life to the service of his country playing an important role within the European Community.

His contribution to the construction of a better world equilibrium will often be cited as an example to be followed. President Pompidou never rejected great challenges; on the contrary, when he was called to serve he
always responded, well aware of his duty to work for the welfare of his fellow citizens.
Mr. Speaker, that man will go down in history as having been the man of great times, the wise man who always sought negotiation rather than confrontation, the man of the happy medium, the man of detente and conciliation.
Mr. Speaker, we all know in this House how difficult it is for the political man to resist the wear and tear of time. Still, Mr. Georges Pompidou managed to keep the high esteem of everyone, thanks to the deep sense of honesty and devotion which characterized him throughout his life.
On my own behalf and on behalf of my party, I therefore wish to pay a last homage to Mr. Georges Pompidou who always pursued his task with the greatest respect for the individual and deepest love for political institutions.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the warm relations between Canada and France are deeply-rooted in Canadian history. It is therefore with special sorrow that Canadians learned of the death of President Pompidou.
He was a statesman whose greatness extended beyond the boundaries of his country as far as the European Economic Community and the world. He was a man who left the imprint of his character and ideas on his times.
On behalf of my colleagues, I extend our deepest condolences to the French people, Madame Pompidou and his family.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON DEATH OF PRESIDENT OF FRANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one is always stricken by the death of a famous man, especially when he was head of state.
The death of French President Pompidou is all the more impressive and particularly afflicting for us because of the historical, linguistic and cultural links between our two countries.
His predecessor, one of the greatest statesmen of the century, passed on to Mr. Pompidou the delicate responsibility of making more harmonious the relations between the Canadian and French governments. In spite of some susceptible dispositions of the Prime Minister of our country towards France, after the now famous events of 1967, we must admit, Mr. Speaker, that Mr. Pompidou showed magnanimity in the circumstances and we must recognize that his actions made possible good and sound relations between our two countries.
For these reasons, the death of the President of the Republic of France afflicts us deeply.
On behalf of all my colleagues and as a French-speaking member from Quebec, I extend to the family of Mr. Pompidou and to all of France my most sincere condolences.
Newfoundland
April 3, 1974

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before us, Bill C-5 intituled: "An Act to authorize the provision of moneys to meet certain capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways System and Air Canada" is evidence that some changes have occurred during the year. In the bill introduced in former years, a very significant word was recurring fairly often and that was the word "deficit". In this bill, Mr. Speaker, this term has been replaced by another, namely, "securities to be repaid". This is fairly more sophisticated and seems rather successful.
Mr. Speaker, although the president of our Crown corporation is always very well paid and several officials have chosen for themselves important positions and applied the planning formula, the results are the same, that is we are virtually facing a fiasco as a result of the incompetence and irresponsibility of the management. And we can always expect the same results. For instance, when it comes to planning, we always find the same incompetence in the field of agriculture and transport as well as in the St. Lawrence Seaway Administration or the Canadian National. Following advanced planning, our country which was a major producer and exporter of goods sought throughout the world has become an importer.
The government planned the system. If fixed quotas and, to be consistent with its plans, went so far as paying western farmers not to produce. This same government even penalized eastern farmers for producing too much. It even mobilized inspectors to visit farms and keep an eye on farmers. In my opinion, the shortcomings in planning result from the very fact that most people responsible for planning are "yes-men".
We all know that, in the private sector, one must not be satisfied with following but must lead the way.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext:
In private enterprise, as I said, we all know that administration officers develop ideas and put them into practice. Anyone anxious to know the difference between private enterprise and public enterprise does not

April 3, 1974
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
need to go out of the country, or even to get into a new field, he can stay on the same "track". One has only to compare the balance sheets of the CN and the CP. The CN operates at loss while the CP shows profits.
In 1973, the CN came before the government begging for credits to plug the $17 million hole. The same year, the Canadian Pacific's balance sheet showed $125 million profit. In the February 12 edition of Le Soleil, one could read the following:
The Canadian Pacific company announced yesterday an unaudited net revenue of $125 million for 1973, including extraordinary items of $6 million.
That is a $29 million increase over 1972.
Mr. Speaker, in 1971 for instance, the CN came before us again with a deficit of $29 million.
In 1968, the CN had tampered with their employees' superannuation fund, had written off a $371 million debt and in spite of all that it still showed a deficit.
During the 60's, the CN tampered and meddled again with the employees' pension fund. They loaned themselves $675 million at 4 per cent interest for 60 years.
Mr. Speaker, the Social Credit members say that the Canadian National, like many other Crown corporations, should be financed through new credits at a low rate of interest. However, we maintain that savings deserve a reward and that the best reward that can be made at the present time is the payment of interests at the market rate.
Moreover, by lending themselves $675 million at 4 per cent, the CN saved $40 million a year, but those savings are at the expense of retired employees and I think that is an abnormal state of things.
If all that tampering gave results, it would be really encouraging but we know the situation remains the same because by financing its operations in a fraudulent way as it does, the CNR remains constantly in the red.
On the pretense of saving, Mr. Speaker, the CNR lays off personnel, neglects the maintenance of its cars and tracks, and trains derail.
A paper tabled in the House earlier this year and submitted by the Canadian Transport Commission indicates, for example, that in the year 1970 the CPR had 60 derailments, and the CNR 193. In 1971, the CPR had 52 derailments, the CNR 192. In 1972, since the figures for 1973 were not available, the CPR registered 80 derailments while the CNR managed to beat its own records with a total of 230 derailments.
All this to say, Mr. Speaker, that those figures prove that there is always room for improvement at the CNR.
In 1973, CNR authorities forgot to order cars. Officials always on holidays forgot that you have to have cars to move things.
Imagine, Mr. Speaker, a dairy producer who would forget to have his cows inseminated.
Imagine a corner-store owner who would forget to renew his inventories.
Imagine a gardener who would forget to sow or a taxi company who would go into business without cars.

Regardless of the business involved, it is obvious that inadequate and irresponsible administration would give the same results.
As a matter of fact, regardless of the business in which they were involved, those businesses would be doomed to bankruptcy unless they managed to obtain a grant as the CNR does every year.
Mr. Speaker, the car shortage is nothing new. The Canadian National authorities have long been aware of it, as was shown to us in previous years.
At that time, the Canadian National invited members of Parliament to information sessions to tell us for instance about the new customer service.
According to the information agents of that time, the service would be greatly improved through the use of a new electronic system.
Since all movement would be directed by the system, they said it would be very easy to control trains and cars.
Simply by glancing at the reports given out by the computers, it would be possible to tell the movement of trains and the numbers of cars in Canada and even in the United States.
Mr. Speaker, in view of the lack of results, we must conclude that the members of this House have simply been had by jokers since, in spite of all the nice promises, there is still a car shortage.
We still give the iron from our mines to the Americans, we export hard wood for Japan's bowling alleys, and, in our own country, we forget to build railway cars.
At the present time, there are not enough cars to move western grain to the east, to move paper and all other kinds of perishable goods in our country. That is the situation. All this simply because we did not think, we did not get the necessary equipment, we did not organize to meet the transport companies' demands in relation with agriculture, trade and industry throughout the country. That is the situation.
Mr. Speaker, this shows a lack of service but it also shows a waste of money. We could prove at any time that the Canadian National spends money for all types of material which is never delivered.
The CN pays for oil to paint bridges which have not been painted in 20 years. But it still receives oil bills and labour bills.
I am quite ready to admit that the railway companies are a public utility and that they should be maintained and improved.
However, I am not willing to admit that we should nationalize the private enterprise to get better service.
In the transportation area, we can also observe how Air Canada and some airports operate.
Last fall, we heard about the way a contract was awarded for snow removal at the Quebec City airport.
Last fall, in November and December 1973, public calls for tenders were issued: four contractors submitted tenders. This invitation to bid involved a three-year contract. The tenders received by the authorities responsible for
April 3, 1974

snow removal at the Quebec City airport were as follows: $265,696, $288,880, $292,129 and $305,623. Although there was a difference of $40,000 between the lowest and the highest bids the authorities of the Montreal regional agency, which were apparently responsible for this contract, managed to grant the contract to the highest bidder. And among the people interested in this contract, there was a contractor from Sainte-Foy in the riding of Louis-Hebert. At that time, this contractor tried to draw his member's attention to what was going on. He also got in touch with the secretary of the Minister of Transport in Quebec City. Personally, I made several phone calls to the office of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand), in Parliament because I thought he was one of those who could help us. I supplied him with the figures I just mentioned. But apparently he could do nothing. As the minister stated in the House and elsewhere, he has lost control. Is it true or not? In any event, we know that to make profits certain things should be done and others avoided.
We all know that if an honest business calls for tenders, it is in the intention of making a sensible choice to its advantage. It is as simple as that and to date nobody has proved to me that paying the highest price was the most economical principle.
And contrary to our NDP friends, who say that the government should nationalize the CPR, I would rather be in favour of merging the CNR and the CPR. Most of the companies doing business in this country and which are successful in business have often merged. Obviously, some positions in the Canadian National management, starting with that of the president, would disappear. However, in my mind, the benefits drawn from an equitable management of the Canadian Pacific will perhaps lead us to consider the implementation of this practice for other Crown agencies.
Since such a merger policy cannot be realized in one day, Mr. Speaker, we may perhaps attempt some other method, which is that the top management of the Canadian National, including the president, be paid a commission.
Because set salaries are the reason for a stupid and losing administration, I think it would be appropriate to implement our suggestions, as members of parliament, so that government succeeds in instilling awareness and motivation in some management officials and in giving them the guts to do a good job in their companies. I believe this country is prosperous enough to support these transport corporations. In my opinion, if stricter measures were applied, the Crown transportation companies could make their services more profitable and efficient and Parliament would be spared the voting of funds which, until this day, we can only compare to welfare payments. I think the situation is most abnormal in a country that prides itself on being rich, prosperous and well administered. Mr. Speaker, to prove ourselves and show that the country is prosperous, that the administration is honest, we will have to go into action without any delay.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members know, this bill has been around for quite some time, almost a year. It is not my intention to unduly
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada delay the progress of it, but I think this situation clearly illustrates the haphazard manner in which the government is managing the affairs of this country. This bill is a bit of a joke because the money provided by it has already been spent. Therefore, it is redundant.
Perhaps we might consider some of the reasons the bill has been around so long. One reason is it has had very low priority on the government's legislative timetable. It has been nothing more than filler legislation. As I said before, the money has already been spent. Members on both sides in committee and in the House expressed reservation about this particular exercise.
The second reason the bill has been around so long is that, for the first time members of the House and the committee have scrutinized this particular piece of legislation. I am not sure whether it is the first time in history, but for the first time since I have been a member of this House, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) appeared before the committee to explain the bill. That was very useful. It gave members a better understanding of the financial structure of these two Crown corporations.
Throughout the committee hearings, it was obvious that a number of the committee members were not satisfied with the financial arrangements that exist for these two major Crown corporations. I believe the Minister of Finance alluded to the fact he would like to see some changes made in the overall financial structure of these two corporations. This suggestion has also been made by previous Ministers of Transport. It is a position which meets with general agreement among the committee members who took part in the debate in the House as well as the extensive committee proceedings that were carried out.
A good number of the committee members were not satisfied with the answers they received from the officials of these two Crown corporations. They were not satisfied with the explanations nor with the fact that on many occasions the officials of these two major corporations refused to give information which committee members were attempting to elicit. The committee members were also concerned about the fact that these two Crown corporations were not utilizing their resources in the proper fashion and discharging the mandate given to them, namely to provide safe, efficient and effective transportation service by air and rail.
We found that these two corporations were engaged in many exotic, collateral ventures which really have no relationship to the matter of transportation services in this country. For this reason, the amendments were proposed at the report stage. We wanted to focus attention on the fact that these two major Crown corporations are not totally discharging the mandate given to them by the people of Canada.
Another major concern of the committee members is the feeling that parliament has no control over these corporations. This feeling came about because in many instances the officials refused to give the kind of information that was being solicited. It was the general feeling throughout the hearings that parliament has no effective control over these corporations.

April 3, 1974
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
With regard to Air Canada, the service and profit picture in relation to the number of benefits Air Canada enjoys in terms of the monopoly it has in this country certainly is not satisfactory to many committee members. Service standards, labour relations within the company, the fiasco at terminal two, sales promotion expenditure and the whole question of administration within that corporation are questions that were not answered satisfactorily when committee members cross-examined the officials. We were not satisfied with the fact that Air Canada seems to be very intent on branching out into allied ventures, such as Comstock. Here again their reluctance to give committee members certain information created an aura of suspicion.
If these corporations are going to be responsible and prepared to effectively discharge their mandate, they must be accountable to parliament and the people of Canada. Otherwise, it is nothing but contempt of parliament. There was precisely that feeling in Committee that the officials were somewhat contemptuous of the committee members.
I could say basically the same about CNR. We certainly gained the impression that the railways are not interested to the degree they should be in discharging their mandate of safe, efficient and effective railroad transportation to the country. Here again we witnessed the fact that they are involved in many allied ventures, ventures which really have no relationship to the business of transportation. It is our belief that CNR should epitomize an effective and futuristic railroad transportation system. If it cannot do that, how in the name of God are we going to create an effective national transportation system by nationalizing another railroad? The government certainly has an obligation to hold these Crown corporations to their responsibilities, to force them to discharge the mandate they were given. If these corporations fail to discharge that mandate they should be answerable to parliament.
This leads me to another point which involves the minister. We have the distinct feeling that parliament is exercising no effective control over these corporations. But the minister is suggesting that he, on behalf of the government, has no control. He says, in effect, that the CTC is an all-powerful, autonomous group which has handicapped him in his activities to a great extent. He also implies he has no control over the railways and goes on to suggest further that in these circumstances the only solution to the crisis in transportation, the only way to overhaul the system, is by nationalizing the Canadian Pacific.
There are a number of myths associated with that assumption. One of them seems obvious to me-it is that the people who favour nationalizing the CP are of the opinion that civil servants can do the job of running a railroad much more effectively than those who are employed by private enterprise. It has certainly not been proven to me that a nationalized concern can offer rates below those offered by a private corporation, and unless supporting facts are brought to the surface, what we have here is nothing more than a simplistic, socialistic solution to a complex major problem.

The minister tells us that transportation is in a mess, and that the policy of the government has been wrong. Indeed, he suggests now that the government really has no policy. This is surprising, because only a year ago the same minister was stoutly defending his so-called policy. In a speech made in this House on June 19, as reported at page 4902 of Hansard, the hon. gentleman is reported as saying: "It must not be said we have not established a policy; we have." Then, he went on to outline the provisions of the National Transportation Act and the role played by the CTC. At the Western Economic Conference held in Calgary last July, he indicated that our transportation system as a whole was one of the best in the world, if not the best. Then, on March 7, as reported at page 268, the same minister stated:
Something we do not have is a rail policy and I hope that sooner rather than later it will be possible to have such a policy.
That is quite an admission. It is really an admission of failure. It is an admission that the past policy of the government has been a failure, an admission that if indeed, there was a policy it has not been effectively administered.
Since this parliament began back in January, 1973, we have been greatly disappointed by the attitude of the minister and by the attitude of the government with respect to discharging their responsibilities in the area of transportation. The minister's answers in the House have been flippant, evasive, confusing. And now we find they are conflicting, because the interpretation he places upon the role of the CTC is diametrically opposed to the interpretation placed upon it by the president of the commission. Only yesterday, in committee, Mr. Benson indicated that the minister has all the power he needs to over-rule the CTC. In these circumstances, I maintain that parliament ought not to put up with this kind of nonsense any longer. The minister certainly has the necessary powers. Whether he wants to exercise them or not is a matter for him to decide, but if he does not wish to exercise them then perhaps Marchand had better march along.
With regard to the minister's power vis-a-vis the Canadian Transport Commission, it might be worthwhile placing on record in categorical terms the authority the minister possesses. Section 64 of the National Transportation Act states:
The Governor in Council may at any time, in his discretion, either upon petition of any party, person or company interested, or of his own motion, and without any petition or application, vary or rescind any order, decision, rule or regulation of the Commission, whether such order or decision is made inter partes or otherwise, and whether such regulation is general or limited in its scope and application; and any order that the Governor-in-Council may make with respect thereto is binding upon the Commission and upon all parties.
That is pretty clear. The minister suggests that this power can only be used in certain circumstances. Yet he has never told us either in the House or in the committee just what those circumstances are.
He also indicates he has no power over the railroads. It is my opinion that the provisions of the Railway Act do give the minister sufficient authority to enable him to compel the railways to discharge their mandate. Subsection 100(1) of the Railway Act provides that whenever the minister is aware that a railway company which has received construction subsidies out of public funds cannot
April 3, 1974

be safely and efficiently operated, he may apply to the Commission for an order that the railway and its equipment, or both, shall be put in a safe and efficient condition. The Commission is authorized to make such an order. The order may direct what repairs, improvements or additions are to be made to the railways, equipment, or both, and stipulate time limits for commencement and completion.
Section 262(1) (c) embodies the standards which an efficient railway must meet. This particular section requires that a railway company shall, according to its powers, without delay, and with due care and diligence, receive, carry and deliver all traffic offered for carriage upon the railway.
Subsections 235(1) and (2) require that a railway company shall, according to its powers, afford to all persons and companies all reasonable and proper facilities for the receiving, forwarding and delivering of traffic. These requirements are mandatory. If a railway does not meet them, it is derelict in its duty and, therefore, not efficient.
Section 3 of the National Transportation Act embodies a policy statement. It declares that an efficient transportation system is essential to protect the interests of the users of transportation, and to maintain the economic wellbeing and growth of Canada. This section states in no uncertain terms that the efficiency of the national transportation system is to be judged by its efficiency in serving the private interests of users of the transportation system and in serving the general public interest, that is, both the private interests of the public and the public interest. The various private interests of the component parts of the transportation system are, obviously, not a factor upon which the efficiency of the system is to be judged.
We could go on. In his various statements made both inside and outside the House, the minister has clearly indicated that the railways are inefficient, that they are not interested in renovating their rolling stock, that the rails are deteriorating, what some of the bridges, even, are falling down. This is not a situation in which one can expect an effective passenger service to be provided. Certainly that, in itself, is an admission, a recognition of the fact that the railways are not functioning efficiently.
I could also refer to section 48 of the National Transportation Act, as well sections 50 and 51. These sections of policy, which is the National Transportation Act and the Railway Act, clearly and unequivocally define the powers of the minister. Evidently the minister has failed to exercise these powers in such a way as to compel the railways to discharge their mandate.
The minister also has the power of the purse, the power to grant money, such as the moneys provided by this particular bill. I suggest that funds could be earmarked for a specific purpose, such as to upgrade the road bed, to upgrade the availability of rolling stock, or to upgrade various pieces of equipment required.
Let me simply say to the minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, that in my opinion he has failed to discharge his responsibilities as Minister of Transport. He has failed to discharge his responsibilities to the people of Canada and to this parliament. I suggest that, rather than hide behind
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada the CTC and the National Transportation Act, he get on with the job of working with the CTC and the railways so that this country can start moving again.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the CNR financing bill gives the House an opportunity to analyse the way the CNR is spending money. The way the CNR spends money is very important to the people of my riding. In my riding there is a huge railway centre in the city of Melville. I also represent a riding that produces a lot of grain and livestock, as well as potash. Therefore, the movement of these commodities is a very important part of our economy.
This afternoon I want to deal particularly with one or two matters of real concern to the people who work on the railway in my riding. I refer to rail safety, a matter the members of this House should really be concerned about, as well as the condition of the tracks that the men have to work on and the branch lines across the prairies.
Over the weekend an extremely unfortunate incident occurred in my riding. A young man who had just started work on the railways was killed when working on a train. He was a member of a crew the CNR were experimenting with, called a survey crew, in an effort to cut down on the number of men from four to three. As a result of this, and due to the track conditions at the time, this young man was the unfortunate victim in a dreadful accident, one that should be investigated by the minister, the CNR and the CTC. The train in question was backing in to hook up to some grain cars when it jumped the rails and caught this man between a railway car and a bin that held some fertilizer.
This incident has caused great concern among railroaders in my riding, as it will among those right across the country. They are concerned about the CNR's handling of matters such as safety, as well as the condition of rail tracks across this country. In my riding on Sunday I met some union officials employed by the CNR who told me that in the previous 30 hour period there were four derailments in the area serviced by the men working out of Melville, largely caused by the condition of the tracks.
I suggest that in examining the financing of the CNR, we should look at some of the problems experienced by the workers and at the dangers to which they are subjected. We all know winter conditions in the prairies, the large amount of snowfall this year, and we all know the condition of the tracks. At the same time, the CNR picks this period to conduct an experimental survey to cut down on the number of men in a crew. The railroaders in Melville and all across western Canada, I understand, are very concerned by this kind of action on the part of CNR officials and management.
I want to take this opportunity to ask the minister and CNR officials to investigate this accident to which I have referred. A person has died because of what appears to me to be negligence, to be a lack of concern about the safety of men and the conditions under which they have to work. The morale of CNR workers is hitting, in my opinion, a level that is probably lower than it has been for many a year. This is due to some of the matters I have already mentioned. When you combine this with the fact that we are now witnessing more difficulty in moving grain than

April 3, 1974
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada we have ever had in this country, then you wonder why the CNR does not examine its methods and policies from one end to the other.
I can very well understand and sympathize with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) when he says that transportation is in a real mess. This real mess includes the running of the CNR, or at least many aspects of the CNR's affairs across this country. The railway men in my constituency tell me that many safety regulations are overlooked by CNR officials. They are told to do things that are clearly against the safety regulations, and they feel that this jeopardizes their lives, their health and physical safety. I think it is about time we examined some of the matters that affect the day to day lives of people working on the railways, something of great importance to them. And not only to them, Mr. Speaker; it is important to the country to keep the economy moving, to keep commodities like grain, potash, lumber, iron ore and so on moving to our factories and markets.
Another matter of deep concern to the people of my riding is the low priority placed by the CNR on maintaining their trackage, not their main line tracks but their branch line tracks in particular, tracks that serve the small towns, villages and hamlets of Saskatchewan along which grain and other commodities are transported. The CNR seems to be forgetting about these tracks. It also seems to be forgetting about what I think is the mandate of the CNR, which is to serve the public of this country regardless where they live, be it in a city like Toronto or a small village, town or hamlet in rural Saskatchewan. The mandate of the CNR is to serve all people equally efficiently; its mandate is not necessarily to serve only those industries or areas of Canada from which they derive a profit. This is a facet on which I wish to put heavy stress.
I have already referred to movement of grain. At the present time we are several thousand boxcars behind meeting our export commitments, particularly on the west coast. These commitments have at stake, I suppose, the reputation of Canada as a grain exporting nation. Also at stake are the incomes of many farmers in the prairies. We are not behind in our deliveries simply because of heavy snowfall; other things enter into the picture, such as the morale of the men, the conditions under which they work, the conditions of the tracks, and the low priority that both CNR and CPR place on the movement of grain across this country. This is a situation that must be changed, and changed very quickly.
One of the other concerns I have spoken about on behalf of the ordinary citizen of my riding is the intention of the railways in this country to abandon many of their branch lines. There may be some lines that could be abandoned, but I think the railway companies are trying to abandon far too many of them, lines that serve a lot of people in rural communities which should not be abandoned. If these lines are abandoned it will mean a real loss both in economics and services to the farmers, small towns and the people living in those areas, so I think the railways should take a serious look at their intention to abandon rail branch lines in this country.

Another concern is the phasing out of station agencies. Many have been phased out in the last few years and many more will be phased out in 1974 and 1975. I will give you one ludicrous example, in my opinion, of a station agency that is to be phased out in my riding. I refer to the town of Ituna, a town of perhaps 1,500 to 1,700 people, which is a good size in terms of the people it serves. I have in mind not only the town itself but the communities surrounding that town which will be affected if the station agency is removed, not only this year, but next year and the year after. This is not a small town of 200, 300 or 400 people, but a place of 1,500 to 1,700 people which serves perhaps an additional 700 people beyond those who live in the town. I see no reason for phasing out a station agency in a place of that size. It is on the main line of the CNR which has some passenger service and over which a lot of goods are transported, so there is no reason for phasing out an agency in a town on a line such as that. This action will not save the CNR much money, but it will create much hardship for the community and the people who live around that community of Ituna. This is but one example of many that we on the prairies and, indeed others in other parts of Canada, could give the CNR, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner).
Those are some of the things that concern my constituents in their day-to-day lives as they consider the operations of the CNR and CPR across the country. I think the Minister of Transport was right when he said that transportation is in a real mess. I think the CNR, in terms of the way it is managed and handled across this country, is also in a real mess. We need some new management and controls on the Canadian National in this country as well as on the CPR.
In conclusion, I would say that in this country we indeed need a new transportation policy that removes freight inequities, which will nationalize the CPR and integrate it with the CNR into one transportation system with new management. Then perhaps we would have a system which could efficiently serve the people of this country regardless of where they live. We need a new transportation system that would be integrated and have service as its motto rather than the making of profit or moving into areas that are more easily handled. It seems to me that the people who work for the CNR usually follow the lead of the CPR. If the CPR is not doing something then the CNR will use that as an excuse, or if the CPR is moving in a new direction the CNR again follows that lead. That seems to have been the pattern that has developed over the last few years. I suggest an amalgamation of the two railway companies, putting them both under public ownership and control, running them efficiently on behalf of the people of this country whether they live in Toronto or in a small town in my riding on the prairies.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is, of course, a very basic philosophical difference between my position and that of the last speaker. I see very little justification, on the basis of past performance, for the nationalization of any additional industry in any facet of our society by this or any other government or by
April 3, 1974

any particular Crown corporation that may presently exist.
Perhaps it is not so much from the point of view of opposition to the financing of the CNR and the Air Canada structure that this bill should be discussed in this House, but rather from the point of view that the behaviour of those in charge of this socialized structure is such that members have been denied the opportunity to express opinions, let alone be part of the decision making process. We have been denied the right to express an opinion prior to the time a deal has become a fait accompli and then presented as part of the financing bill for the CNR and Air Canada.
Parliament is thus denied its proper right, and the public at large their right to know what is becoming of federal money, and how it is being spent. The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) outlined this in great detail. I think his remarks should be considered almost classic and referred to frequently by members of this House who have any concern whatsoever for the expenditure of our public moneys and the knowledge that the public is entitled to prior to such expenditure. This has been denied to the House.
The committee which has met in respect of this bill is another mockery of the opportunity for a member elected by the public to participate in the economic structure of this country. When one has an hour and a half or perhaps two hours twice a week over a three or four week period to discuss an item of the significance of this one, certainly that is virtually no opportunity at all to get an intelligent idea as to how one should express himself on behalf of his constituency in particular, and Canada in general. Yet, this is just another example of how the committee procedure of this House conceals from the public the knowledge of their own affairs.
The transportation system, under the public ownership structure, has been subjected to pressures of a political nature. This has made it virtually impossible for the system to either serve the Canadian people or make a profit on their behalf. It has been compelled, perhaps at some expense, to build the hotels which have been criticized. It has been compelled by the public and political pressures to render services which were not economic. The House is further compelled, as a result of these political pressures, to annually underwrite the losses which the public ownership vehicle has accrued over the years. At no time has there been any directive, publicly noted, from the government saying to this publicly owned structure: It is your responsibility to both serve and to make a profit; it is your responsibility to at least render service to Canada at a minimal cost and prove that you have exercised proper efficiency in your managerial practices on behalf of the Canadian public. It has been some time since there has been any indication that the government has directed the transportation system of this country to give consideration to the necessary national requirements in respect of development, the basic reason for the initial construction of our present transportation system. The challenge of that responsibility has not been met.
At a recent transport committee meeting which did not deal with this particular bill we found ourselves almost completely frustrated in an effort to obtain information in
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada respect of the operation of the railroads, in respect of the function played by the Canadian Transport Commission, and in respect of the authority that can and should be exercised by the minister. We found we were in a virtually helpless position with ineffective legislation and less effective administration, and the combination of the two spells out the death knell of any long-term transportation policy in Canada's best interests.
We find that in this bill continuing evidence to support our belief that there is proliferation of the infringement upon the private world by public ownership. There seems to be no justification given by the Department of Transport for authorizing the railway to invest in de Havilland or in any other industry as it may desire or for authorizing Air Canada to invest in the aerospace industry without an examination of the long-term profitability or the longterm advantage to the Canadian population by virtue of this participation. These are the things which give me great cause for concern as this bill is about to become law by virtue of the vote that will be taken. There is no way this House can deny the funds which have been spent. They must be granted, but it is with great regret I say this when I see the infringement of the parliamentary right of members of this House to participate in the structure of the nationally owned transportation system we have.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) does not seem to have any grave concern about the development of the port structure of this country. Whether you are from Vancouver or from Saint John, whether you are in a fishing port or on the St. Lawrence seaway, it seems that Port development is allowed to coast. Its relationship to national development is not given proper consideration. We might consider, for instance, the opportunity we have to develop the port of Saint John and the opportunity Canada has to develop with it. With its railroad connections, the port of Saint John could be developed as a container and other type of port for the benefit of the whole Canadian economy. This has not been considered by the Minister of Transport. Apparently no money is to be made available for a major development in this area. Are we to be served on the Atlantic coast by another domain merely because our government fails to recognize the value of this port to Canada and to the whole east coast of North America.
This House and the Department of Transport will dillydally until we learn that somewhere along the coast someone chose to build an island to create a port to service the east coast of the North American continent. With a little initiative on the part of this government such development could be created at the port of Saint John for the benefit of all Canada. It would provide service to all the people of the east coast of this continent. This plan, however, is not forthcoming. The view of the government today is land locked. The government looks inward at development in the main metropolitan areas of Canada and cannot see the relative value of the periphery of this country as it plans its policies in respect of transportation or anything else.
I am very much concerned about the basic operation, for instance, of Air Canada. At one of the meetings of the transportation committee we heard a great song and dance

April 3, 1974
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
about the capability of Air Canada to handle air freight and its intention to develop this business. We heard how it had pioneered in this business and had sought it from one coast to the other in Canada to serve the world. The lobster industry of the province of New Brunswick took up the challenge. It expanded its market opportunities. It sent its salesmen throughout the world. It developed markets. The result was a very major increase in the income, particularly of the lobster fishermen on the Atlantic seaboard. Now, we find there is no possibility of any guaranteed space in the Air Canada freight structure. We find that the lobster industry has become so thoroughly disgruntled with the service rendered by Air Canada that it is seriously considering moving its base of operations to the Boston area so that it may obtain service from foreign carriers for Atlantic provinces' products because this service cannot be obtained otherwise.
I wish the Minister of Transport were here. He has been noticably absent from this House during the entire debate to the detriment of transportation and his portfolio. Bear in mind that this market to which I referred was developed because Air Canada, in the promotion of air freight, offered an opportunity to an industry on the Atlantic coast which has virtually been withdrawn because the service offered cannot be maintained. Remember the lobster industry shaped itself for the benefit of Air Canada's freight operations. We are asked to pass this bill while an engineering fiasco is taking place in the harbour of Saint John. I shall not go into this in great detail. However, it is virtually a fiasco. The government of Canada failed to undertake its responsibility in respect of harbour development at Saint John, but insisted upon laying on the engineering structure under which the province of New Brunswick would pay the bills. Perhaps the Minister of Transport should make an all-inclusive statement to this House in respect of the fiasco which has developed.
We are being asked to pay the bill while in my constituency a branch line of one of the railways is being considered for closure. This branch line happens to serve an area in which a new fish plant has been built, where a paper mill is being expanded and where a confectionery industry needs the transportation facilities. I think there is some discussion under way about the closing of this branch line. Apparently a branch line closure can take place at the whim of the railway. The Canadian Transportation Commission has made no comment in this regard. There is merely a rumour that this is to take place, but no suggestion has been made that hearings will be held concerning the needs of the area served and the transportation situation generally there. Neither the commission nor the minister appear to have authority. So, we pour hundreds of million of dollars into a system which the people of the country own but over which the public has no control.
Yes, the money must be voted, but we should not allow this organization to run helter-skelter through our dollars while it continues to do what it sees fit without any control being exercised over it by the House of Commons or the people of Canada. We see the socialistic tendencies and the bureaucratic attitudes which exist. We have the aerospace industry. There is plenty of money for that, although it could very well come from the private enterprise sector. The same situation exists in respect of the business of providing shelter. However, when services are

needed for national development, we are denied the moneys required for this by this government and the province of New Brunswick loses faith in the loyalty of the government to its people and the members from this area.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak briefly on Bill C-5, the CNR financing bill. Although I spoke during second reading, I feel there are a few additional comments I should make so far as a transportation policy for Canada is concerned. We are presented with a bill like this every year, and members have an opportunity to discuss the transportation problems which effect not only their own ridings but various other parts of the country. Yet during the period that I have been a member of this House I have not seen too much progress made in updating and upgrading our national transportation system. In fact, the minister expressed this rather ably not too long ago when he said transportation policy in general was in a mess.
There are a few points I would like to make. I believe other hon. members have raised them, but I think we should again request that action be taken along certain lines. One of the points repeatedly brought to my attention by railway workers in my area concerns the need for better railway line maintenance. The lack of proper maintenance has led to a number of derailments, not only in Kootenay West but in other areas across Canada. There is growing concern on the part of railway workers that the situation in becoming worse.
Just the other day hon. members received copies of a very interesting brief submitted by the Canadian Railway Labour Association, stressing the need for something to be done with respect to safety on our railway systems. It is a matter that has appeared in numerous reports. The railway workers are requesting that something be done to ensure that we examine the safety factor in a much more critical way than we have in the past.
I am convinced that the Canadian Transport Commission should be doing a lot more to ensure that safety measures are carried out, particularly measures respecting maintenance. I wish to read several paragraphs from the railway workers' brief because they outline the problem very clearly.
There is a growing concern about the number of derailments and other accidents which occur on railways. One aspect of this problem is the fact that railways are not required by law to make public the reports of its officers concerning the cause of accidents. Section 225 of the Railway Act requires that railway companies and certain of their employees report to the Canadian Transport Commission in respect of certain kinds of accidents and their causes.
The law also provides that the Commission may, by regulation, declare the manner and form in which such information will be given, the class of accident to which the law applies and that information given in compliance with the law may be declared privileged.
The Commission (Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada) gave effect to this law by promulgating General Order 0-1. In addition to setting forth the details about the making of reports the Order contains Section (6) which reads as follows:
Every accident report, or information respecting the same, furnished the Board by any railway company pursuant to the provisions of the Railway Act and of this Order and the report of any person appointed by the Board to inquire into and report upon any accident
April 3, 1974

or casualty occurring on any such railway is declared to be privileged and shall only be made public or given out by Order of the Board.
The Canadian Railway Labour Association takes exception to section 225 and General Order 0-1 on the grounds that the law and regulations effectively prevent our Association from determining the reported cause of certain railway accidents and efforts to assure that adequate steps are taken to prevent a recurrence ...
We do suggest, however, that the Minister of Transport should take an active interest in the problem to ensure that changes are made which will meet the public need for information concerning the cause of railway accidents while protecting the legitimate interests of the railways.
The point being made is that the railway unions have difficulty in obtaining reports on the causes of accidents. As a result they are not in a position to effectively deal with the railway companies, or the government, by having certain methods of operation improved. This is a very serious matter. People working on the railways whose lives are endangered are entitled to this information. In this way the unions can seek to protect their members. I know that in some cases this may be privileged information, and that some of it may have to be held back, but basically there is nothing wrong with the general public, and in particular the men who man the trains, receiving this information and taking up with management the question of changes that should be made to ensure that more accidents do not take place.
Just the other day before boarding the plane to return to my riding I received a telephone call from one of the railway unions at Nelson in connection with an accident. Several cars had gone off the rail line. I was told there was not too much traffic on this particular line, and that the railway company was not interested in having the repair work carried out for a couple of weeks. At the top end of that line, Mr. Speaker, there is a mill which ships lumber and chips to market by rail. As a result, the jobs of a number of workers were at stake. Such an attitude on the part of big railway companies is not good. The Transport Commission should check on problems like that to make sure the railway companies no longer get away with the things that they have been able to pull over the past few years. I hope that over the next few months the minister, the government, and the CTC will take action with respect to safety in the maintenance of tracks.
There is another point that I have been pressing for a number of years, and on which I feel we should have an amendment to the Railway Act. It deals with the transportation of natural resources from Canada. I raise this so that when general transportation policies come up for discussion, these things will be brought to the attention of the minister and the government in the hope that some changes can be made.
A number of years ago in British Columbia, a provincial railway was granted a charter by a previous provincial government. It was called the Kootenay and Elk Railway and it was a phony, if you want to put it that way, because it had no rolling stock of its own, no engine, caboose or cars. It was incorporated for one reason only, to take the coal from the east Kootenay region of British Columbia down to the American border where it hooked up with an American railway line for connection with the Pacific
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada coast. Fortunately, the present NDP government in British Columbia stopped this railway by a simple process. While it had a charter and could have built line, it was not allowed to go through Crown lands.
I have spoken many times in an effort to have the government take action to stop the building of this Kootenay and Elk line from the coal fields to the American border because of the loss of 600 or 700 jobs. The same thing could happen in any part of Canada, for instance on the prairies, where they could haul wheat to one of the U.S. rail lines to be transported to the Pacific coast. They could take potash or any other raw material. It is my position that when we have national rail lines in Canada our goods, wherever possible, should be hauled on them. This should be the objective of our national transportation policy. The act needs to be amended to make certain that the same situation does not take place in some other part of Canada as that which was attempted with the Kootenay and Elk Railway. I am going to suggest to the minister that he look into the possibility of amending the legislation to ensure that we never get into this bind again.
I have just one further point to make before I sit down, Mr. Speaker. When we talk about national transportation, we mean not only rail transportation but air and every other type of transportation. It seems to me that over the past years very little has been done by our national rail lines in the area of passenger transportation and I do not think they receive much encouragement from the Department of Transport or the Canadian Transport Commission. In my area, the Kettle Valley line runs through the southern part of British Columbia to the coast. Some sections have practically been abandoned and passenger traffic is non-existent. This has happened all over the country, of course.
When we look around at other nations like Japan and some countries in Europe, we find that the transportation systems are being upgraded and great numbers of people are using the trains. A similar policy has to be adopted in our own country. We are facing an energy shortage and there is no doubt that a great deal can be done and could be done if the two large railway companies were prodded by a government that was really interested in improving passenger service. To subsidize an inefficient line whose trains travel a few miles per hour is a sure way of killing passenger traffic in Canada. In many instances this is deliberate and the railways make it so awkward to get a meal or a berth on their trains, and journeys take so long, that people have stopped using them. We should insist that facilities be upgraded.
I have just one more point in closing, Mr. Speaker. We have heard a great deal about raw materials coming to southern Canada from the north and there has been talk of rail systems and of studies being made. I would suggest again that the appropriate committee of this House thoroughly check the possibility of rail connections with the north. We can bring oil, gas and minerals from the north with an efficient rail system and goods could be transported to the north much more cheaply by air.
I urge that this House and the appropriate department conduct an investigation along these lines very soon. I am not going to say anything more except that I hope we are going to see some action regarding the safety and upgrad-

April 3, 1974
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada ing of our railway lines. I should like to see a start made this year.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it appears that I may be the last or the next to last speaker in this debate on third reading of the CNR financing bill. I wanted to make a few remarks about the railway's operations and the kind of financing that is being done. It is my opinion that the amendments proposed by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) and his colleagues early in this debate were designed to hinder if not destroy a Crown corporation. They complain about Air Canada buying 30 per cent of Wardair, but I doubt if the same people would have objected if Canadian Pacific had been buying instead of Air Canada.
The hon. member for Vegreville complained about the CNR and Air Canada not fulfilling their mandate and meeting the transportation requirements of Canadians. I agree with him. I think he is perfectly right and that both of our national railways have failed, since World War II, to keep up with the growing transportation needs of the country. The growth in the movement of goods and people has not been met by the railway systems, private or public. I should like to say more about that in a few moments, and I hope that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) will be back in his seat by then because I should like to have his comments.
The hon. member for Vegreville says that the CNR and Air Canada are not fulfilling their mandate, and I agree with him, but I want to say that the reason for this is perfectly understandable and logical. I would have thought that he would have realized that, with the kind of transportation policies we have had under successive national governments and the kind of transportation act that we have, Canadian National Railways and Air Canada do not operate any differently from Canadian Pacific Railway and CP Air. All operate within the same framework and on the same ground rules, that is on the basis of competition and profitability. There is little difference between their methods of operation. This makes me sad, because the CNR is not operating as a publicly owned and controlled corporation should operate.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Vegreville believes that the idea of nationalizing the CPR is simplistic and socialistic. I repeat: transportation is an essential public

service. The field is a natural monopoly, and therefore must be classed as a public utility. A transport system operates best in the public interest when it is publicly owned and controlled. Another hon. member on my right complained earlier about parliament and the government not having control over our publicly-owned railway and air carrier. Indirectly, he was trying to say what I am trying to say. A publicly-owned and operated transport system must be under public control. This has been the experience of other governments of the world, conservative, liberal, communist, socialist or what have you. Rail and air transport systems in most countries, regardless of political stripe, are publicly-owned, operated and controlled.
I want to say a word about some moves made by our sort of supernumerary minister of transport, the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. He announced a program for the emergency movement of grain. My goodness, the CPR was even to run four more trains in an attempt to meet targets. I do not know if the minister in charge of the Wheat Board consulted the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marehand), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) or the Canadian Transport Commission before giving his blessing to something both railways have been doing since Christmas, namely, abandoning branch lines in western Canada which were blocked with snow. I am not aware of any permission given by the Canadian Transport Commission for the railways to abandon such lines. Some branch lines have not had trains on them for weeks and weeks, some not even since the new year. There are thousands of country elevators on those branch lines which are full of grain. What did the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board do? He gave his blessing to the railways, allowed them to abandon those branch lines, and told farmers that they are to undertake longer hauls, which means that they will need to go to alternate delivery points or further, to main line shipping points.
The problem with that kind of plan is that starting this week or next week, municipal and provincial officials will place bans on the use of our municipal roads and highways for certain purposes, so farmers will not be able to haul grain to the nearest delivery point, let alone to the alternate delivery point. Again, the minister in charge of the Wheat Board is doing things backwards. The Minister of Transport, or some CTC official, or even railway officials, should point out to the minister in charge of the Wheat Board what is likely to happen. The railroads should be instructed to make extra efforts to clear these branch lines of snow and empty the elevators of grain, because if this does not happen the farmers will be in trouble. They will not be able to haul away their grain. I hope that my good friends on the other side of the House will point out these facts to the minister in charge of the Wheat Board and put a stop to the nonsensical program he initiated a few days ago.
As the Minister of Finance is present, I want to talk about the subject matter of the bill. This is last year's CNR financing bill. No doubt another financing bill to cover this year will be brought in shortly when the government House Leader needs a bill to fill in time. These financing bills are pretty well identical, although the money amounts may vary. There is little evidence to show that money is to be spent on different priorities. The Minister

April 3, 1974
of Finance may recall that I asked him in the House a number of weeks ago if consideration was being given to the problem of handling the Canadian National debt, and whether consideration was being given to its refinancing. Paraphrasing his answer, he said that this matter was being looked at again. I should appreciate it if he could elaborate on that answer today.
Since the Second World War both our national railways have not placed enough emphasis on spending money on the improvement of roadbed, track, the acquisition of rolling stock, and on locomotives, with the result that events have caught up with them. It will take several hundreds of millions of dollars of expenditures to update and improve to a good standard thousands of miles of roadbed and track and to acquire thousands of pieces of rolling stock, by which I mean not just boxcars, but also refrigerator cars, livestock cars and so on. In addition, they must buy enough locomotives to meet demand at all times of year. In committee, I asked the former president of Canadian National, Mr. MacMillan, just before he took his well-earned retirement, if he would ask the board of directors and management of CNR to look again at priorities and examine again projected needs for rolling stock and locomotive power for the years ahead. Obviously, the railway has allowed its stock of rolling stock and locomotives to fall below what it ought to be, and this fact has caught up with it.
Before bringing in the CNR financing bill for 1974-75, I wonder if the Minister of Finance would meet with the Minister of Transport as well as the managements and boards of Canadian National and Air Canada, and discuss all these things. Let him see if he can get from the railway a commitment to put a higher priority on doing those things I have mentioned, as our transport facilities need updating and enlarging. Even though this may involve an expenditure of another couple of hundred million dollars in next year's financing bill for improving track, buying new rolling stock and locomotives and improving yards in Vancouver and Thunder Bay and for improving track at Churchill and Prince Rupert, it will be well worth it. At least we shall do something to put right the errors which the railways have committed during the last 20 years. I hope the minister agrees that my request is reasonable. Surely, the railroad should place a higher priority on meeting its operating requirements than on the acquisition of real estate or other esoteric projects.
If this is not done, we will still be in the same mess this year, next year and in years thereafter, and the Minister of Transport, poor man whoever he may be, will still get up and talk about the confusion and inadequacy of our transport policy and our National Transportation Act. If the minister asks the managements and boards of CNR and Air Canada to place higher priority on the purchase of new equipment which will improve service, I think, when this sort of bill is debated next time round, he will receive a much more sympathetic hearing from all sides of the House and the bill will be given speedier passage.
I am sure the minister is probably tired, as are many other members, of hearing the same complaints every year. The CNR financing bill would be an excellent mechanism to begin to redirect the priorities of the railway and
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada Air Canada. It may then lessen some of the complaints, so the next financing bill would get more support and an enthusiastic welcome from members, particularly those on this side of the House. I know the minister would miss hearing the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner), the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) and myself making railway speeches every year. That will only come about if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) brings in a much better and, if necessary, larger financing bill in the next few weeks.
In closing, I want to repeat my main point. We cannot meet Canada's transportation needs until our major modes of transportation, rail and air, are returned to public democratic ownership and control. I emphasize the word "control" for the benefit of the hon. member for Vegreville. They should be operated as any public utility is operated. We must forget about the nineteenth century railroad baron-profit way of running a railroad.
It is illogical to think you can properly operate a transportation system with competition and profit as the objectives. It is an essential public service. It is just as illogical as attempting to operate two competing sewer and water systems running under a main street or two competing highways. If one were to follow the argument of the hon. members to my right to a logical conclusion, we would return to the 1830's and have competing toll roads, owned and operated by private enterprise. If anyone suggested that, they would be laughed out of town. They would certainly be laughed out of this House.
The time has come to integrate our rail and air transportation system with other modes of transportation, including bus and water transportation. When we do that, we will be on the road to a transportation system suitable for a country as large as ours, with a northern climate and thinly scattered population. We will be able to do something about equalized or subsidized or a combination of both, passenger fares and freight rates. We will be able to put an end to discrimination against some people because of where they happen to be located in this country. We might be able to arrange it so that someone can fly from Toronto to Inuvik for the same price as someone flying from Toronto to Winnipeg. It might be possible to purchase a quart of milk in Yellowknife at the same price as in Regina. Over half the price of milk in the north is the cost of transportation.
In this way low and middle income families in the north will be able to purchase the quantity of an essential food which they should be purchasing. With a system of equalized and subsidized rates for essential food and other commodities, people all over the country will be treated much more fairly and equitably. This would do as much for national unity as anything else which members on the government side talk about repeatedly. This has continually been a sore point among people in Atlantic, western and northern Canada.
I am not suggesting that what we in the New Democratic Party propose would be 100 per cent right, but I am suggesting it is the only alternative left. We can no longer tinker with a little bit of public enterprise here, private enterprise there and a combination of both somewhere else. Surely, we have learned our lesson by now. What we have is not working as it should be. The only alternative is

April 3, 1974
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
a publicly-owned, operated and controlled public utility for our rail and transportation system in Canada.
