speechtext:
It is a serious problem for the province. In any event, I apologize to Your Honour for the momentary confusion about me deferring or not deferring to the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner). Because of the tangled history of this particular piece of legislation, it was to be expected this confusion would arise, even at this point in time.
Bill C-5 has been an interesting focal point for many months for opposition members to show how inept and generally incompetent this government has been in such a routine matter as financing our two main Crown corporations. I do not intend, as some members opposite have suggested, to filibuster at this point, but I wish to make a few remarks that may be relevant. If nothing else, the proceedings to this point in time have shown the curious reluctance of not only the people who make the policies for our Crown corporations, but the management of Air Canada and CNR to be frank and honest with members of parliament from all parties who are attempting to find out their policy guidelines and what their key officials are doing.
Some members feel it is a pity that our terms of reference did not include the power to have officials of CPR appear before our committee. I certainly agree with that contention. I notice, for example, that the earnings of CP have shown a considerable increase in the past year. May I quote from a newspaper article to illustrate this point:

The company said record earnings for Canadian Pacific Investments, substantial increase in income from the Soo Line Railroad and marginal raises in CP Telecommunications income were "more than enough to offset the lower earnings of rail, highway transport and containership operations, attributable, in varying degrees, to the effects of the strike of Associated Non-Operating Railway Unions".
We on this side have suggested it would be beneficial if CNR would get back into its primary role of moving goods and people cheaply and efficiently, and forget about some of their more esoteric roles like building hotels, getting into the aerospace business and getting their finances mixed up with Air Canada. I think it is only fair to suggest it would be a good thing if the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) would have a serious look at encouraging or directing CP to divest itself or well, to some extent at least, of those associated enterprises which might distract it from its primary role of moving goods and people efficiently. It seems to me the reluctance to disclose precisely what the railways and Air Canada are doing is carried over into other areas beside the area of management responsibility.
For example, last November a study was released indicating that rail costs in connection with moving Alberta coal into Ontario markets were much less than those quoted by Canada's two major railroads. The Ontario minister of transport and communications told the legislature the study indicated that computed unit train costs-I do not know whether this is the correct way of putting it- were at least 35 per cent lower than the rates quoted by CN and CP rail. Surprised by this information, the minister said that Alberta coal was substantially more competitive in the Ontario market than had been previously believed. He went on to say that if CN and CP did not disclose unit train costs he would press the Minister of Transport to conduct an inquiry. To my knowledge, though, the information in question has not yet been disclosed. It is still being awaited by those government officials and by the Canadian public. This is symptomatic of the lack of control exercised by the Minister of Transport over the railway companies and other transport agencies.
Since this bill was introduced the minister has stated very frankly that he does not possess either the authority or the overall policies which would enable him to do his job properly. If the minister really believes he lacks authority, a view which is apparently not shared by the President of the CTC, let the government bring forward amendments to the legislation, and do so quickly. I see no reason why the support of most members of the House should not be expected.
As to the financial aspect of Bill C-5, I should like to stress the apparent lack of leadership forthcoming from the government over the last several years. When he appeared before the committee, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) addressed himself to some extent to the question whether it would be advisable to separate the financing of Air Canada from the financing of the CNR. He stated that while he himself was not close to this particular issue he could tell the committee that it had not come before cabinet in any concrete form. He added "I could not tell you what the policy dispute is. All I am
April 3, 1974

saying to you is that if there were a reasonable proposition to split the capital structure, I think it would be a good idea." Well, that seems to be a straightforward statement by the minister and one with which I happen to agree.
The President of the CNR takes an opposite view, and while he is entitled to do so the question does arise: Who is running the financing of the CN and Air Canada? Is it the government of Canada, as I think most Canadians would like to believe, or is it being run at the whim of the executive officials concerned? Mr. MacMillan made an interesting comment when he was asked to define the primary role of the CN. The discussion had centred on whether the CN was paying sufficient attention to moving people and to moving commodities. He stated in the course of his most recent appearance before the Committee on Transport and Communications:
I think it would be quite wrong for us to restrict ourselves to rail movement because in that way the public is not properly served. The future, I think, .will go even further into the intermodal methodology of handling business.
"Intermodal methodology"; that is a very interesting term and we would like to know exactly what it means. Unfortunately, so far, we have not been able to find out either from the President of CN or from the President of Air Canada what they consider their basic guidelines to be. Mr. Pratte is on record as saying on several occasions that he is not certain what the primary role of Air Canada should be and it appears that Mr. MacMillan is also confused to some extent. Perhaps not, but that is the way it appeared to me, as a member of the committee.
The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) stated quite clearly in his speech today that he felt the Minister of Transport does have sufficient authority to direct the affairs of the nation's carriers to the extent he feels they should be directed. In support of his argument, my hon. friend quoted from the Railway Act and the National Transportation Act and gave examples of what could be done. For some reason, the minister has been reluctant to crack the whip and assert the authority he possesses by virtue of existing legislation.
I conclude by saying that, if in fact the minister honestly feels he needs more authority in order to expedite a solution of Canada's transportation problems he should, without delay, bring forward the necessary amendments to the National Transportation Act. It is not as though this were a new situation. It is not as though the government has not had time in which to act. It is not as though this were not a matter of great importance to Canada. As I mentioned earlier, the lack of a transportation policy at federal level has tremendous implications for the future of our regional development programs, particularly in eastern Canada, since in the absence of an efficient and comprehensive transportation policy any meaningful efforts to reduce regional disparity are doomed to encounter needless complication and expense.
Once more, I ask the minister and his cabinet colleagues to remedy the situation which they themselves have caused, and to bring forward quickly any legislative changes which they feel would help to bring Canada back into the forefront as far as transportation generally, is concerned. We do not stack up too badly when it comes to certain aspects of moving commodities but judging from
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada the complaints which come across my desk, as far as moving particular commodities is concerned, it appears we are getting into as bad a situation with regard to moving timber, potash, wheat and apples as we have been in for years when it comes to transporting people. This situation must change before it deteriorates any further, because if the present rate of decline is allowed to continue the effect on our economic development will be very serious.

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS AND AIR CANADA
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES AND DEBENTURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other night when the amendments to Bill C-5 were up for discussion I dealt mainly with the question of rail transportation. On third reading I should like to deal briefly with some of my thoughts about the lack of an air policy in this country of ours.
I listened to my socialist friends to my left speak of nationalization, and this reminded me of our study of this particular bill in committee last year when the question of the government, through Air Canada, acquiring Wardair was being discussed. I tend to think a fabulous price was being asked for a 30 per cent ownership in Wardair. Wardair did not have any planes of its own. It ended up owning one DC-9 and an old Bristol freighter, leasing the remainder of its aircraft. But what the committee study boiled down to in regard to Air Canada buying Wardair was: What did Air Canada really want from Wardair? The answer given by the president of Air Canada to the committee was: "Charter flight know-how".
Never before have I seen a Crown corporation admitting it did not have all the answers and was prepared to go to private industry to buy know-how. To me this is a prime example of why nationalization and socialism will eventually fail. It will fail because it will fail to stimulate and germinate any new thoughts. Approaches become narrower and narrower. To me this was a great admission that nationalization and socialism is not the answer, no matter whether it be in regard to air operations, rail operations, industry or what have you. Eventually, it will have to be admitted that socialism stifles initiative.
One might ask, how has initiative been stifled in Air Canada? Some time ago I spoke in this House about Air Canada owning Viscounts and flying them for 22 years when no other airline could afford to fly them. They were nice, safe little planes. I felt secure when I flew in them. But their fuel costs were astonishing. Today a 747 can fly just as cheaply as a Viscount, yet Air Canada flew them for 22 years. I suggest that is narrow thinking on the part of a Crown corporation. They should have gone out and bought know-how far sooner than they did when they thought of purchasing Wardair.
What else is wrong with our air policy? The other evening I pointed out that the National Transportation Act of 1967 was deficient, and I said so at that time. I roundly debated it with the then Minister of Transport, Mr. Pickersgill, and I still think the act is deficient. But Mr. Pickersgill did create the CTC, and a job for himself. In all fairness to Mr. Pickersgill, in 1966 he did produce a workable solution to part of our air policy when he brought in what is commonly referred to as our regional air policy.

April 3, 1974
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
Our two main line carriers are Air Canada and CPAir. CPAir has about one-fifth the number of planes Air Canada has, yet it turns in a profit. This particular measure is to cover debts incurred by Air Canada of $140 million and a recurring debt of $13 million to pay for engines for the Lockheed 1011-and I will be dealing with that in a moment.
Our second largest carrier, as I say, is CPAir, with very limited routes in Canada. A year after we gave Alitalia the right to fly into Toronto from Rome and Naples, the government finally made up its mind to give CPAir the right to fly into Milan. That year of delay and indecision on the part of the government without a doubt cost CPAir quite a bit of traffic from Italy to Toronto, and from Toronto to Italy for that matter. Delays cost private industry money. Delays caused by government, whose tentacles reach out into every corner of private industry, cost private industry a huge amount of money.
Today we have our two major carriers and five regional carriers, and as I said in 1966 the regional air policy is a workable one. The five regional carriers are relatively sound. Air Canada had the bulk of the routes and could fly into any city in Canada, but declared it was losing money on short hauls. It claimed they were too expensive to operate and that they should be given to some of the regional carriers. The regional carriers took them up and made money from them. Pacific Western has grown to the point where it will soon join the big two. Transair, Nor-dair, Quebecair and Eastern Provincial are all doing very nicely. I have a question I should like to ask my socialist friends to my left. If a nationalized Air Canada cannot make money flying short hauls to the small cities of Canada, how can private enterprise prosper from the same routes? I think my friends to my left should analyze that situation.
Let me move one step further in our air policy. There are something like 125 different carriers smaller than the regionals operating in Canada. The regionals now have grown so big they all use DC-9,s or the equivalent 737's. But they either cannot or do not want to fly to some of these small towns, particularly in northern British Columbia, the Northwest Territories, Yukon, some parts of northern Quebec and so on, and these 125 carriers are begging the government to make a decision on a third line carrier policy. The third line carriers are hamstrung today by government regulations, and they want the government to make a decision so they will be allowed to operate services which are very much required. In the committee the other day Mr. Benson, president of the Canadian Transport Commission, was asked what was the government's policy on third line carriers. He replied that it was not for him to develop government policy, but he had been asked by the minister to assist in developing such a policy. I say that is not good enough. There will be continued delay. This government body is trying to grant licences and make rules under a policy that does not exist.
Only recently a third line carrier was granted permission to fly into Grande Prairie, Alberta. This third line carrier would have been very happy with this decision, but the CTC placed so many regulations on the operation that it has made it practically impossible for this third line carrier to operate that particular route. I am referring to

Time Air, a small third line carrier that flies from Medicine Hat-Lethbridge-Calgary-Red Deer-Edmonton and which wants to extend its service into the Peace River area. It is a worth-while enterprise that does not make any large amount of money but provides a needed service to smaller cities in Alberta. Since the Canadian Transport Commission under Mr. Benson does not know what licensing policy to apply, it gives Air Canada the right to fly into Grande Prairie, but ties it up so badly with regulations that in fact it cannot fly into Grande Prairie. This is why we need an air policy that will work.
This lack of a policy is causing financial harm to 125 smaller carriers which are providing necessary service in our northland, or what you might call our hinterland, no matter what part of Canada that may be, in the Maritimes, Labrador, Quebec, Northern Ontario, the northern part of western Canada or the Northwest Territories. We must have a policy statement from the minister saying that the third line carriers will be allowed to serve these areas. The regional carriers are now so strong that the third line carriers could not compete with them even if they had the desire. That is all the third line carriers are suggesting. They are suggesting that if they can provide the service into a place like Grande Prairie, a service which the regional carrier is now providing, it should be given the opportunity to do so. They are not going to fly in with a DC-9 as Canadian Pacific or Pacific Western is now doing, they will fly in with a smaller plane perhaps a little more often than the regional carrier would do.
This indecision on the part of the government is causing the Canadian taxpayers to provide this service to the small consumers at a cost of thousands upon thousands of dollars. It is all right to say that by 1980 or the year 2000 we will all be living in 11 cities in Canada. That may be nice, and many experts have propounded that theory, but I do not believe it. I believe there will be lots of Canadians who will want to live in smaller regions throughout Canada rather than in 11 major cities. These smaller communities need the service, and in some instances to an even larger degree than do the larger cities. For example, how do you get to Inuvik or Yellowknife unless you go in by air? How do you get to some of the smaller centres in British Columbia unless you go in by air?
These third line carriers are being hamstrung by regulation upon regulation. Some of these regulations can not even be cleared away by the Canadian Transport Commission. Mr. Benson the other day made a lengthy statement about his concern for the airline carriers, but he said he could not do anything for them because he did not know what government policy is and it was not his job to devise it. Mr. Benson and I have always been cordial with one another, but I have never been a great admirer of his thinking. However, in respect of that statement I go along with him. It is not his job to devise policy, it is the job of the government and the minister. This minister is bogged down with problems of grain transportation and it is the government's responsibility to help him out. He should be moved to some other portfolio which he can handle, or he should be given a smart executive assistant or a smart parliamentary secretary who can devise policy for him.

Give him a sabbatical leave, that would not be a bad idea. Surely, the government must face up to the responsibility that it is it's job to devise air policy which will coincide with the development of this great country of ours. We should not have a policy that will tie up CPA on the Milan route for a year and not tie up the regional carriers which are fairly successful. They should be given some bilateral agreements in respect of Canada and the United States. Eastern Provincial should be allowed to fly to Boston and some other areas in the eastern United States, and Pacific Western should be able to fly into Los Angeles and other areas in the western United States.
The third line carriers should be allowed to provide service to any of these smaller centres; that is not asking too much. The minister shakes his head and says he has no transportation policy, and he is right. We have no transportation policy, we have no rail policy and we have no air policy, yet this Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) asks the House to pass this bill. It is only effective to July 1, 1974 so out of pity I suppose it will be passed, but it would not be passed if it were handled by the Department of Transport. If this bill were being presented by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) I think it would be a sin to pass it. He admits he does not know what he is doing with the money and does not know where he is going.
Air Canada is buying up the aircraft manufacturing business. It will buy out de Havilland and tie itself down to one type of aircraft. The Minister of Finance knows very well that this idea of STOL aircraft will not work. This scheme to operate STOL aircraft between Montreal and Ottawa is not a workable scheme. There is some suggestion that we should build another airport just north of Montreal. We do not need another airport in downtown Montreal and we do not need another one in downtown Ottawa. It is only a 20-minute drive between the present airport in Ottawa and Parliament Hill, traffic permitting, and we certainly do not need another airport here.
When you come right down to it, with fuel costs going up in the world the way they have been it is cheaper to move poeple by train over relatively short distances. I think the cost of moving people by air versus train is about 15 to 1. We are spending millions of dollars deciding whether or not we need a new airport at Pickering. Mr. MacMillan has suggested that if we give him the $800 million required to build this airport at Pickering, he will build straight track between Montreal and Toronto and beat the airlines all the way in moving people. I believe he could do so.
We have been caught up with this air transport idea. We have said to heck with the railways, we must give Air Canada all the money it wants for all the expensive aircraft it needs. I am not particularly impressed by the new 1011. Many reports have suggested that this aircraft is not going to prove workable. I read about one the other day flying into Calgary two and a half hours late. I suggest in fact this aircraft has flown into Calgary late more often than on time. What the problem is I really do not know, but I question this expenditure for the purchase of the 1011 type aircraft. This is a new type and Air
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada Canada felt it had to have it, so it put in an order for a lot of them. I suggest that the most popular type of aircraft in the United States for years is a type that Air Canada is just now beginning to buy. It has just placed orders for this type, so it is behind the times. Again I have the idea that socialism stifles thinking; it does not expand it. Socialism will never have the capability that free enterprise possesses given an equal opportunity. Certainly, it will never have the capability of free enterprise as long as we have governments that cannot make up their minds.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) announced, I think in 1972, that the government intended to purchase 30 per cent of the de Havilland company in relation to this STOL scheme. I think this was an election announcement. I saw that at the time as an election gimmick designed for the voters of Montreal, and I saw it as a wrong step. He and I normally agree on most things.

Mr. Speaker, what I want the government to do is so clear and straightforward I can say it in a very few minutes. I suspect the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) knows what

April 3, 1974
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada
I am about to say. In fact, he told me a while ago he could make the speech himself. My answer to him is I hope he will go out and make the speech to the Canadian National and also to the Canadian Pacific. Mr. Speaker, this is the third day of April. Here we are into the fourth month of 1974 and there has not yet been any 1974 cost of living escalation in respect of the pensions of retired railway workers either Canadian National or Canadian Pacific. Almost all pensioners whose pension plans are under the aegis of the federal government are now receiving cost of living escalation benefits and in all cases where those benefits are paid they no longer are limited to 2 per cent per year but are made equal to the actual percentage increase in the cost of living.
The Canadian National is an emanation of this government. We are now in the process of voting the Canadian National a rather large sum of money. I contend it is time for the government to tell the Canadian National to get in step with other government operations. It is also my view and that of my party that the Canadian Pacific Railway, although it is called a private company, is at work in the public domain, exists because of public support, and should be told likewise. In other words my request, my insistence, is that the government use its authority, its muscle if necessary, on behalf of the retired railway workers both Canadian National and Canadian Pacific and any others such as those who draw their benefits from the old provident fund or who were employed by some of the companies scattered around the country.
I am aware of the fact that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) on several occasions promised the appointment of a commissioner to examine into all aspects of railway pensions having in mind both the pension provisions for those still working and the pensions of those retired. That is good. I want to see that implemented just as soon as possible and when the commissioner goes to work he can deal with such questions as the formula for calculating railway pensions, which ought to be on the basis of 2 per cent for each year of service. He can also deal with the question of the amount of pension that is payable to a widow and other such changes as need to be made.
But, Mr. Speaker, we do not need to wait for a commissioner for the word to be delivered to these two major railways systems that the railway pensioners should not be asked to wait any longer for a 1974 cost of living escalation. The word I get-you know, we sometimes get word which is correct or may not be totally correct-is that the Canadian National is ready to provide a cost of living escalation and is prepared to do so in accordance with the rise in the cost of living and not just 2 per cent. However, for some reason or other the Canadian National is holding back. One speculative reason is that the CPR does not want to go along. I do not think the CNR should wait for the CPR. On the other hand, I think the government should talk to both of them. I plead very strongly, as I have on other occasions over the past several decades, for the rights of our railway pensioners.
We thought we had won the battle for the right of an annual escalation of pensions. This is happening now with a great many cases. I think it is completely unfair, extremely wrong and a case of a miscarriage of justice, if you will, that these retired persons, widows and others

have to wait for the escalation of their pensions. I plead therefore with the government not just that the Minister of Finance can say he knew what I was going to say but that he use his muscle as Minister of Finance when he delivers to the Canadian National this money we are voting and say to Norman MacMillan and the CNR, "Increase the pensions of your retired employees in accordance with the rise in the cost of living; we want no monkey work and no delay".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has again raised the problem of pensions which are currently under negotiation, a problem which is causing a great deal of concern. However, I presume that this matter will be satisfactorily settled.
The manner in which we have carried out this financing of Canadian National and Air Canada over the years really does not seem to be in the interests of developing an adequate transportation system. In this piece of legislation we are repeating the sins of 30 years ago. We are allowing Air Canada to go into commerce an investment portfolio. If ever there was anything which loused up transportation and ended Pierre Burton's dream it was when the railway companies ceased to be railway companies and became investors in everything from land to hotels, to the point where today we do not have adequate rail service to meet our needs, either from the CNR, the CPR, or from both of them in combination.
Now, we are going to allow Air Canada to open its own investment portfolio, and we will lend it the money to do so. It seems idiotic that we should repeat the mistake that we made with the railroads, and that we should not learn from our history in that regard. It might be advantageous for the minister himself to set up another Comstock company, or to manufacture airplanes, but I certainly hope he will not allow Air Canada to do this. Air Canada will never go back to using either the single engine or twin engine Otter, and therefore I do not see any reason why it should become involved in the manufacture of such planes.
I also suggest that if Air Canada is not able to make money on the charter business itself, then the least it should do is buy Wardair out, particularly if Wardair has all the expertise in that field. Why have Air Canada just invested in that company? Why not buy it out completely? Most people believe Air Canada was established and financed by the government to provide service by flying airplanes on behalf of the Canadian people. It was not really set up to make a profit. I repeat that it was set up to provide service to people, but with every day that goes by it is drifting further and further away from that objective.
The hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner), who represents a rural area somewhat similar to mine, is well aware of the problem we face in air transportation. Really, the government has no air transport policy. It has established an air committee which decides on who gets the licenses. Under the Canadian Transport Act, the minister has the right to override such decisions, and occasionally does so, although so far as I am concerned this is not necessarily done in the interests of the public but for rather obscure reasons.
Air Canada and all other major carriers are well supervised, but this does not hold true with respect to the lower categories. For years Air Canada had to fly from the west through Kapuskasing, North Bay, through to Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal, but for a number of years it has not had a connecting route from Northern Ontario to western Canada. The only exception was a route between Toronto and Montreal going through the northland of Quebec and Ontario. But it was interesting when a third class carrier
1138

April 3, 1974
Canadian National Railways and Air Canada made an application, and that application was granted, little support was given by Air Canada to see that that carrier received the same assistance that is provided to a national carrier in an integrated system.
In my part of Ontario we make our air reservations through a Zenith number, using Air Canada. Air Canada can make an arrangement for reservations with Nor-OntAir which is a wholly owned subsidiary of Northland Transportation, and therefore of the Ontario government. For the other carrier operating between Sudbury, North Bay and Ottawa, Air Canada connot and will not make arrangements for connections. One has to make reservations from northern Ontario via Sudbury and Toronto to Ottawa. This may add to statistics but it does not do anything to transport people in northern Ontario. If a service were available through the national carrier who is already part of the intervention in the transfer of passengers, the people of the north would use it.
Several months ago in committee we heard the president of Air Canada speak about this, and he said that it would not pay to put a service between Montreal, Ottawa and Sudbury. Nordair, the regional carrier is an integral part of our system and should be given the same kind of treatment which would allow them to fulfil a role in an organized and orderly fashion. When Air Canada said they were not prepared to provide the service, Nordair made an application and now we understand that Air Canada is going to apply as well and probably will put in a service from Montreal, Ottawa, Sudbury, Thunder Bay and on to Winnipeg via a northern route.
We have provided Air Canada with money and cushy jobs on the board of directors, although the president does not seem to really know what they do. Perhaps the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) should have all these vicepresidents removed rather than provide $3 million to buy expertise from Max Ward. If we really need the knowledge that Wardair has in order to run a charter system for Air Canada, let us hire Mr. Ward and some others and make them vice-presidents or even the president of Air Canada. If we have a subsidiary, let us make it possible for it to make more money than it is making now or we will just be using it to provide Air Canada with a class of traffic that it is not able to carry now.
After next June, the minister will be introducing another CNR financing bill. We have probably been involved in this exercise three times in 1973-74 and hon. members would be interested in knowing how the financing is being used. Hon. members will agree that railways in Canada should be operated for the service of Canadians, whether with passenger service or freight and other services normally provided by a railroad. But now we are building all kinds of assets for the Canadian National Railways such as this needle that has been mentioned. Now, it may be that with a mast on top it will provide a new public communications system but, Mr. Speaker, that is not running a railroad. In the early days, telephone lines were laid along the railways and therefore the railways got into the communications field. There may be some merit in this, but I think they spend more time on it than they do on developing their services.

One of these days the railroads will be nationalized as public utilities. They will operate trains and probably have stations and maintain track. This bill will not accomplish any of those things but is going to create for Air Canada the same problems that were created for the Canadian National Railways. It is for this reason, Mr. Speaker, that I am opposed to the passage of this bill. Probably it is a necessary bill although there was a three-year period when the railways operated without the bill being passed and seemed to manage quite well. I suggest to hon. members that if we examine the operation of our railways and national air service, we will find many deficiencies in the service. It is not so much the money involved in paying for the transportation that concerns us but what we get for that money. We have not received much for it over the last 20 years. If we allow Air Canada to have an investment portfolio they, too, will fritter away whatever small brain power there is at the top of the organization through developing things not connected with air transportation.
